newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya to host Zaire mini-summit as rebels advance.
newsitem.headline: Kenya to host Zaire mini-summit as rebels advance.

text.p: Kenya hosts a mini-summit on Wednesday on war tearing Zaire apart but diplomats said a breakthrough was unlikely without the rebels, Uganda and Rwanda.
A Kenyan foreign ministry spokesman said Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo was expected in Nairobi later on Tuesday to attend the summit as representative of President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Also attending the Nairobi talks would be Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi, Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe, Congolese President Pascal Lissouba, South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki and President Paul Biya of Cameroon, the spokesman added.
Diplomats said even with Kengo the meeting would find it hard to win a push for a ceasefire and political settlement in the absence of representatives of the rebels, Rwanda and Uganda.
Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire rebels contest Kenya's role as an honest mediator, saying Moi wants to prop up his friend Mobutu.
Kenyan officials gave no dates for the subsequent regional summit -- called Nairobi Three -- but said it would be soon after Wednesday's meeting.

Kenya, South Africa, Zimbabwe and Cameroon were mandated by the Nairobi Two summit last December to lead African efforts to end the fighting in Zaire, where rebels have captured a fifth of its territory including the city of Kisangani at the weekend.

Since then, Kabila's forces have advanced on several fronts and are reportedly targeting mineral-rich Shaba province and Mobutu's northern jungle palace at Gbadolite near the border with the Central African Republic.
Organisation of African Unity Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim arrived in Nairobi and will join U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun at the meeting from Wednesday as observers.
Salim said leaders would examine ways of ending hostilities in Zaire and pushing ahead with a political settlement.
"In any conflict it is important to first call for a cessation of hostilities. We want to examine how the hostilities could be ended and a political process started," Salim said.
Mobutu, Zaire's ruler for 32 years, was invited but is being treated for cancer in Monaco and has been out of his country for much of the time since the rebels launched their revolt last October.
"This meeting is a build-up after others. The meeting will assess the mood in the Zaire conflict and gauge whether a subsequent full-blown summit on Zaire can be arranged," one diplomat said.
Zaire's government had insisted on a withdrawal of all foreign forces from east Zaire and an international monitoring force to confirm the pullout before attending Nairobi Three.
Zaire accuses Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of sending their troops to fight alongside rebels. All three deny the charges.
Analysts said the absence of South African President and Africa's elder and revered statesman Neslon Mandela was a sign he doubted the success of the Nairobi meeting without Mobutu's participation.
Mobutu sought to rally his crumbling government against the advancing rebels from the east on Monday by telephoning his ministers from his hospital bed in the Riviera principality of Monaco.
Kabila, who rejects a ceasefire before negotiations about ending Mobutu's rule, made a diplomatic breakthrough in his search for recognition when Mandela received him in Johannesburg on February 26.
